summary: Be An Earth System Trend Detective! Wildfire response is still mostly reactive: resources move after ignition. SEDE ("thirst" in Portuguese) moves the decision before the fire. Using NASA Earth-observation data, it computes Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD), the measure of how thirsty the atmosphere is and how fast it pulls water from soil and plants, to flag vegetation that is drying into fuel. A retrospective module links past VPD patterns to past ignitions, and a predictive module projects short- and medium-term VPD trends to map rising desiccation risk. The method works in any biome, from the Brazilian Cerrado to temperate forests. It matters because wildfires drive smoke-related health risks, biodiversity loss and food and commodity price volatility. An alert before the fire lets civil defense, brigades and environmental agencies place prevention resources where they matter most.
details: How it works: air temperature and relative humidity give VPD (VPD = es − ea; es = 0.6108·exp[17.27·T/(T+237.3)] kPa; ea = es·RH/100). SEDE adds evapotranspiration and vegetation context and compares each region with its own history. Retrospective module: identifies the climate patterns and exact conditions that preceded past ignitions. Predictive module: projects short- and medium-term VPD trends to map desiccation risk before fires appear. Output: a ranked list of critical regions with VPD level, trend and alert level (Critical, Attention, Monitored). Benefits: lead time for prevention, a region-agnostic method, and an accessible tool for civil defense, fire brigades, environmental managers, government agencies and researchers. Tools: NASA data, an interactive project page (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) and a concept interface prototype.
